Additive manufacturing compression overmolding process: (a) Binder jetting of tensile and shear specimens for the designed metal insert with star shaped hooks, (b) Big area additive manufacturing of carbon fiber reinforced polyamide-6,6 (40% wt. CF/PA66), and (c) Compression overmolding of polymer composite on top of metal lattice to obtain the hybrid panel. The process described above was performed to obtain the overmolded hybrid specimens using different metal designs. However, the flowability of the polymer composite into the metal lattice was observed to be very poor. The overmolded hybrid panel of 4 mm thick is shown in Fig. 3.3.4(a). The metal inserts can be easily peeled off from the polymer composite and thus they can be separated as shown in Fig 3.3.4(b). The features of the metal insert are too small for the long fiber thermoplastic to flow into it. Hence, the long fibers are not flowing into the metal inserts and causes improper mechanical bonding. This can be seen in the insert of Fig. 3.3.4(a). Since the 40% wt. CF/PA66 LFT did not penetrate through the metal insert with the star shaped hooks, 20% wt. CF/ABS SFT was considered as an alternative to investigate the metal insert design. 8 | P age Figure 3.3.4. Flowability of carbon fiber reinforced polyamide-6,6 (40% wt. The metal-polymer panels obtained by overmolding 20% wt. CF/ABS on binder jet tensile specimens through a similar AM-CM process are shown in Fig. 3.3.5. The CF/ABS preforms fabricated via robotic arm extruder (refer Section 3.1) are preheated in Protherm oven at 3430 C for 6 minutes on each side. The heated preform was then moved to be placed on top of the metal tensile specimens and compressed under 70 ton-force for 1 minute. The consolidated specimen after the compression is removed from the press as shown in Fig. 3.3.5. The hybrid panel removed from the press is allowed to cool down at room temperature. LIGHTWEIGHT SEAT DESIGN In this section, the design of restraint integrated 1st row seatback of Ford’s V713 program to make it lightweight while satisfying the mechanical performance requirements is discussed. The seatback shown in Fig. 4.1 (a) is currently manufactured using traditional stamping process where tool and die surface of stamping press forms the flat metal sheets into a net shape. The metal stamped parts are assembled through welding at multiple locations and using bolted connections to the entire seatback frame assembly.
